column2: Outside, your phone always knows where you are. But step inside a big building, and GPS goes quiet.
On our own campus, new students and visitors can easily lose their way.
So we're building Via for our college. It gives you directions inside a building, using just your phone, in three simple steps: pick, scan, and follow.
First, pick where you want to go.
Then scan the nearest marker. It's just a printed sticker on the wall, and the phone instantly knows where you are.
Now follow your route, drawn on the building's own floor plan, and worked out right on the phone.
If you need a route without stairs, choose step-free. If you would rather take the stairs, choose avoid lifts.
And when your route changes floors, the app shows you exactly how you get there, in three D.
Clear steps guide you all the way to the door. And if you take a wrong turn, just scan any marker, and your route starts again from there.
And in beta: scan once, then simply walk, with every turn read aloud.
Under the hood is a corrected, bidirectional Dike-struh search. Our first E S P thirty-two version took a longer route on thirty-six of seven hundred and fifty-six trips.
Today, every pair of places gets the shortest route, and a hundred and ninety-two automated tests keep it that way.
And it all works offline, with no GPS, no Wi-Fi, no beacons, and no server.
Each block is set up from its own floor plan, and shared as a single file.
Next, we want to map every block on our campus, in one shared map library.
Beyond campus, it can help hospitals, malls, airports, and exam halls. And one day, you could walk through a building once, and let it map itself.
It started with a microcontroller and a cloud database. Now, all it takes is a phone, and a sticker. Via. Find your way, anywhere indoors.
Watch the floor map rise into three D, as your dot rides the lift up to the next floor.
